name: The Scales of Ma'at
powers: Weighs the heart of the dead against the feather of truth in the judgment hall.
description: The great balance set up in the Hall of Two Truths, where the heart of the dead was weighed against the feather of Ma'at before Osiris, with Thoth recording the result. Chapter 125 of the Book of the Dead describes the rite, while the devourer Ammit waits to swallow any heart found heavier than the feather. The scene is among the most reproduced images of Egyptian religion.

name: The Feather of Ma'at
powers: The counterweight of truth against which the heart of the dead is weighed.
description: The ostrich feather worn on the head of the goddess Ma'at, placed on the scales of judgment as the counterweight to the heart of the dead. A heart lighter than the feather passed on to the afterlife; a heavier one was devoured by Ammit. The feather, also worn by the god Shu in his role of lifting the sky, became the emblem of a life measured by truth.

name: The Golden Falcon of Hierakonpolis
powers: The earliest great image of the falcon god Horus.
description: A gold head of the falcon god Horus found in the main deposit of the temple at Hierakonpolis, dated to about 3100 BCE, one of the oldest large cult images of a deity to survive from Egypt. With its obsidian eyes and worked gold feathers, it stood as the focus of worship at the site where the Narmer Palette was also found, marking the beginnings of pharaonic divine kingship.

name: The Sistrum
powers: Its rattling pleased the goddess and drove away hostile powers.
description: A sacred rattle of looped bronze rods strung across a frame, shaken in the cult of Hathor and Isis to please the goddess and repel evil with its hissing sound. Priestesses, queens, and kings bore it in temple ritual, and great ceremonial versions stood as temple furniture. Its naos-shaped variant carried the cow-eared head of Hathor between its handles and remained in use into Graeco-Roman Egypt.

name: The Crook and Flail
aliases: Shepherd's Crook and Flail of Osiris
material: Gold and blue faience (mythic and royal)
powers: Signs of kingship and of Osiris's shepherd-care over the people.
description: The crossed crook (heka) and flail (nekhakha) carried by Osiris as emblems of royal authority and of the shepherd's care for his flock, laid crossed over royal mummies. Temple reliefs show the living pharaoh handing the pair to the god of the dead and receiving it back, and gilt examples were buried with kings such as Tutankhamun. Together they fix the image of the enthroned Osiris.

name: The Solar Barque of Ra
powers: Carries the sun across the sky by day and through the underworld by night.
description: The two celestial boats in which the sun god Ra sails: the day barque Mandjet crossing the sky and the night barque Mesektet crossing the Duat, where the crew repels the serpent Apep with spears. The nightly battle myth inspired real solar barques buried beside temples and pyramids, including the Khufu boat, so that the king might make the same journey after death.
source: Pyramid Texts and solar barque burials

name: Ushabti Figurines
powers: Answer the summons to labor in the afterlife in place of the deceased.
description: Small mummiform figurines placed in Egyptian tombs to perform field labor for the dead in the afterlife, inscribed with spell 6 of the Book of the Dead, in which the figure answers 'here I am' when summoned to work. A single burial could hold several hundred, from a modest clay set to the 413 ushabtis of Tutankhamun. The name derives from the Egyptian word for 'answerer.'
source: Book of the Dead, spell 6; tomb assemblages

name: The Djed Pillar
powers: Symbol of stability and of the backbone of Osiris.
description: The columnar sign shaped like a stylized tree trunk or spinal column, symbol of stability and of Osiris, whose backbone it was said to be. Set up as a temple emblem and raised by the king in the sed festival to renew his reign, it was also worn as an amulet; in the myth Isis and Nephthys restore the god beside it. Countless faience djed amulets survive from graves.

name: The Knot of Isis
powers: Guards the wearer through the power of Isis.
description: The looped red tjet amulet, the 'girdle of Isis,' worn by the living and the dead for the goddess's protection. Spell 156 of the Book of the Dead directs that it be made of red jasper and placed on the neck of the deceased so that Isis's might guards the throat. Red carnelian and faience tjets are common in New Kingdom burials, where they sit with the djed and ankh in protective groupings.
source: Book of the Dead, spell 156; amulet deposits

name: The Uraeus
powers: Spits fire against the king's enemies; guards the brow as the eye of Ra.
description: The rearing cobra worn on the brow of the pharaoh and of deities such as Ra, embodying the goddess Wadjet, protector of Lower Egypt. The uraeus spat fire at the king's foes and stood for the blazing eye that defended the sun god, and it was worn by kings and gods alike. Golden examples survive on royal diadems, most famously the cobra and vulture of Tutankhamun's gold mask.

name: The Senet Board
powers: Its play mirrored the soul's passage through the hazards of the afterlife.
description: The Egyptian board game of thirty squares in three rows, played with counters and knucklebones, the most common game board found in Egypt. The crossing of its hazardous squares mirrored the soul's journey through the afterlife, and the Book of the Dead shows the deceased playing senet against an invisible opponent to win passage. Complete boards, including Tutankhamun's, survive from royal tombs.
source: Excavated boards; Book of the Dead vignettes

name: The Palette of Narmer
powers: Ceremonial record of the king's victory and of the unification of the Two Lands.
description: A ceremonial siltstone palette from Hierakonpolis carved around 3100 BCE, showing King Narmer smiting an enemy and reviewing decapitated captives, long read as an early record of the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt. The falcon-god Horus perched above a bound foe and the king wielding a mace set the visual language of pharaonic royal power for three thousand years.

name: The War Shield of Neith
powers: Emblem of the goddess of war and of weaving.
description: The emblem of the goddess Neith of Sais: a shield across which two crossed arrows are set, combining her natures as a war goddess and a weaver. The symbol is attested as her sign from early Egyptian writing, painted on her temple walls and on votive objects, and the classical authors Plutarch and Herodotus described it. It is one of the oldest goddess emblems of Egypt.
source: Neith emblem on early votives; Plutarch, De Iside

name: The Wesekh Collar
powers: Bestowed solar protection and divine favor on its wearer.
description: The broad beaded collar worn across the chest by pharaohs, queens, and gods, built of rows of faience and semiprecious beads capped by golden falcon-headed terminals. Such collars were given as royal gifts and buried with the dead, who are shown receiving them from deities; Tutankhamun's burial yielded dozens in gold, glass, and stone. The wesekh lent its wearer solar protection and divine favor.

name: The Cup of Jamshid
powers: Reveals the whole world to the one who looks into it.
description: The cup of the legendary shah Jamshid, in which, according to the Shahnameh and later Persian tradition, the whole world could be seen as in a mirror, so that nothing was hidden from the king. The cup became a byword for far-seeing royal wisdom, and Persian poets used it as an image of mystical vision and self-knowledge. Its ties to the older idea of the king's divine glory are debated.

name: Rostam's Spear
powers: The heavy lance carried beside the mace and lasso in the hero's trials.
description: The heavy war-spear of the hero Rostam in the Shahnameh, carried alongside his bull-headed mace and lasso through the Haft Khan and the wars against Turan, and used to strike down champions in single combat. In Ferdowsi's epic it is one of the enormous plain weapons that suit his strength, wielded in duels such as the fateful fight with Sohrab. Its details follow epic convention.

name: The Feather of the Simurgh
powers: Burned as a signal, its smoke summons the great bird to help.
description: The feather given by the great bird Simurgh to the hero Zal and later to his son Rostam, to be burned whenever they needed the bird's aid, at whose smoke Simurgh came flying. In the Shahnameh the feather carries the abandoned boy Zal to safety and later rescues Rostam in his direst need. In later Sufi poetry it became an emblem of the soul's reliance on divine help.

name: The Mace of Faridun
maker: Forged for the young prince Faridun
powers: Struck down the tyrant Zahhak and freed Iran from his reign.
description: The bull-headed mace (gurz) forged for the young prince Faridun, which Ferdowsi describes being made to his measure before his campaign against the tyrant Zahhak. With it Faridun struck Zahhak's crowned head and split the serpents on his shoulders, ending a thousand years of tyranny and binding the usurper in a mountain cave. It became the archetypal weapon of Persian hero-kings.

name: The Derafsh Kaviani
material: Leather apron, gold, silk, jewels (later ornament)
maker: Kaveh the blacksmith; ornamented under Faridun
powers: Royal standard of Iran, carried before the shahs as a sign of popular revolt and kingship.
description: The leather apron of the blacksmith Kaveh, raised on a spear when he led the people of Iran against the tyrant Zahhak; the new king Faridun then adorned it with gold, silk, and jewels, and it became the royal standard of the Shahs under the name Derafsh Kaviani. The banner is retold each Newroz with Kaveh as a symbol of popular revolt and rightful rule.

name: The Belt of Tahmineh
powers: Binds the bond between the lady of Samangan and the hero Rostam.
description: A belt said to be woven by Tahmineh of Samangan, mother of Sohrab, and given to the hero Rostam on the night of their meeting, binding their union in some tellings of the tale. The motif varies across recensions of the Shahnameh and in modern retellings, and Ferdowsi's text describes no single canonical belt, so the object's particulars rest on later tradition rather than the epic's own lines.

name: The Arrow of Arash
powers: Its single flight fixed the boundary between Iran and Turan.
description: The arrow shot by Arash the archer from the summit of Mount Damavand to fix the frontier between Iran and Turan, a flight blessed in the myth by the giving of his own strength, covering hundreds of miles before falling on the far bank of the Oxus. Ferdowsi and earlier Persian sources recount how Arash was chosen for the feat, and modern poetry revived the story as a symbol of national sacrifice.

name: The Seal of Solomon
material: Gold ring set with a stone (mythic)
powers: By its engraving of the divine Name, its bearer commanded the winds, beasts, and jinn.
description: The signet ring of the prophet-king Solomon, engraved with the divine Name, by whose power he commanded the winds, beasts, and jinn in Jewish and Islamic tradition alike, told in the Quran, the midrash, and the Thousand and One Nights. Its seal, often drawn as a six-pointed star, later became a widespread protective emblem across the Middle East, North Africa, and Europe.
source: Quran; midrash; Thousand and One Nights

name: Solomon's Flying Carpet
powers: Carried the king, his throne, and his court through the air on the wind.
description: The carpet of Solomon, woven of silk and green stuff, said in Islamic tradition to be large enough to bear the king, his throne, and his whole court, carried through the air by the wind at his command and shaded by a flock of birds overhead. The Quran records the wind as made subject to Solomon, and later commentators expanded this into the famous flying carpet, whose details grow in the tellings.
source: Quran; al-Tabari; al-Kisa'i; Thousand and One Nights

name: Aladdin's Lamp
powers: Rubbed, it summoned a powerful jinni who granted its holder's wishes.
description: The lamp of the tale of Aladdin, added to the Thousand and One Nights by Antoine Galland from the Syrian storyteller Hanna Diyab around 1709. Rubbing it summoned a powerful jinni who granted wishes, while its twin, the magician's lamp, drove the plot's theft and recovery. No medieval Arabic original of the tale survives, so the lamp is a literary invention of the folk tradition.

name: The Magic Carpet of the Nights
powers: Bore its riders through the air to distant lands.
description: The flying carpet of the Thousand and One Nights cycle and of later oriental folklore, a woven rug that carried its riders through the air to far-off countries. Within the Nights corpus itself the carpet appears chiefly in the tale of Prince Husayn in the later 'Forty Wazirs' addition, and much of its modern fame comes from European retellings. Its details vary widely from one telling to another.

name: The Bottle of the Ifrit
powers: Held a vast ifrit imprisoned for centuries until a fisherman freed him.
description: The sealed copper bottle cast up in the fisherman's net in the Thousand and One Nights tale of the Fisherman and the Jinni, from which a vast ifrit escaped in a pillar of smoke and threatened to kill his liberator. The fisherman tricked the spirit back into the vessel by doubting that so great a being could fit. The jar is the archetype of the bottled-jinn motif in world folklore.
source: Thousand and One Nights, The Fisherman and the Jinni

name: Sefer Yetzirah
maker: Tradition attributes it to the patriarch Abraham
powers: Describes the creation of the world through the Hebrew letters and the ten sefirot.
description: The earliest surviving Hebrew text of Jewish mysticism, the 'Book of Formation,' which describes how the world was created through the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet and the ten sefirot, and sets out paths by which the mystic may emulate that act. Its opening lines attribute it to the patriarch Abraham, and it shaped the whole later development of Kabbalah.

name: The Temple Menorah
powers: The seven-branched lampstand kept alight in the sanctuary.
description: The seven-branched golden lampstand of the Tabernacle and later of the Jerusalem Temple, prescribed in the Book of Exodus as a beaten-gold work with almond-shaped cups and blossoms, kept burning in the sanctuary. Its image survives on the Arch of Titus relief and throughout Jewish art, and its fate after the Temple's destruction in 70 CE became a theme of Jewish legend and diaspora memory.
source: Book of Exodus; Arch of Titus relief

name: The Ark of the Covenant
powers: Carried before Israel and kept in the Holy of Holies as the throne of God's presence.
description: The gilded chest built at Sinai to hold the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments, carried before the Israelites and kept in the Holy of Holies of the Jerusalem Temple. Legend holds it was hidden before the Babylonian destruction, while Ethiopian tradition claims it rests at Aksum. Its descriptions come from the biblical books; no archaeological witness survives.

name: The Brazen Serpent
powers: Healed the Israelites bitten by desert serpents when they looked upon it.
description: The bronze serpent made by Moses at God's command to heal the Israelites bitten by serpents in the wilderness, raised on a pole so that the stricken who looked upon it lived. Kept in the Jerusalem Temple, it was later destroyed by King Hezekiah as an idol under the name Nehushtan. Its story is told in Numbers and 2 Kings, and the object itself is known only from scripture.

name: The Sword of Goliath
powers: The heavy blade of the Philistine champion, kept as a relic at Nob.
description: The sword of the Philistine champion Goliath, taken as spoil after David slew him and later kept wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod at the sanctuary of Nob, where the fugitive David received it, saying there was none like it. The weapon is described in the First Book of Samuel, and David's possession of it anchors his kingship narrative in the biblical account.

name: The Khamsa
powers: Deflects the evil eye and brings blessing to its bearer.
description: The open-hand amulet of the Maghreb and wider Middle East, called the Hand of Fatima after the Prophet's daughter and the Hand of Miriam in Jewish usage, hung in homes, worn as jewelry, and painted on doorways against the evil eye. The silver khamsa was the standard talisman of North African Jews and Muslims alike, with pieces from sheet silver to fine filigree set with coral.

name: The Gris-gris
maker: Fqih (learned man) who wrote the contents
powers: Protects, heals, or brings luck by the written words sealed inside.
description: A small leather pouch worn on the body, holding written Qur'anic verses, prayers, or magic squares, used across North Africa to protect, heal, or bring fortune. In Morocco the hirz was stitched by a fqih and worn at the neck or arm, its power resting entirely on the writing sealed inside. The custom is documented in ethnographic surveys of Maghrebi folk practice and survives today.
source: Ethnographic surveys of Maghrebi folk practice

name: The Tunisian Fibula
powers: Fastened the shawl and served as a bridal heirloom and protective talisman.
description: The large silver pin or brooch, often triangular with a central coral or enamel stud and a long pointed pin, worn by Amazigh women across Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco to fasten the shawl and passed down as a bridal heirloom. Its form echoes Roman-era brooches of the region, and its silver and coral decoration is documented in museum collections of Maghrebi dress.

name: The Sword of Antar
powers: The great blade of the warrior-poet, wielded in his duels and tribal wars.
description: The sword Dhami, the chosen blade of Antarah ibn Shaddad, the pre-Islamic warrior-poet of the Arabian Peninsula whose exploits fill the medieval romance Sirah 'Antar. In the sira, Antar wins the sword in combat and carries it through the wars of the tribe of Abs and his long struggle to marry Abla. The romance is literary, and the sword's named exploits grow with the telling.

name: The Jambiya
powers: Symbol of honor and manhood; drawn in the bara' dance.
description: The short curved dagger with a broad double-edged blade worn at the belt by Yemeni men, a symbol of honor and manhood carried from youth and drawn in the bara' war dance. Silver-sheathed jambiya hilts, some of rhino horn, are treasured heirlooms and marks of tribal standing. The weapon is attested across Yemeni material culture and in the dances, songs, and poetry that surround it.
source: Yemeni material culture and ethnographic records

name: Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi
powers: Said to command the wind and fell whole fields of grass; one of the Three Sacred Treasures.
description: The legendary grass-cutting sword drawn from the tail of the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi by Susanoo, then offered to Amaterasu and placed among the Three Sacred Treasures of the Japanese imperial regalia. Kept today at Atsuta Shrine in Nagoya, it is said to command the wind and cut down an entire field of grass in a single stroke.

name: Yata no Kagami
powers: Reflects truth and brilliance; part of the imperial regalia.
description: The Eight-Fold Mirror hung from a sacred sakaki tree outside the cave where Amaterasu hid, its brilliance luring the sun goddess back to illuminate the world. Revered at Ise Grand Shrine as one of the Three Sacred Treasures, it stands for truth and for the imperial line's legitimacy in Japanese myth.

name: Yasakani no Magatama
powers: Symbolizes benevolent fortune and the sovereign's right to rule.
description: The curved jade bead (magatama) dangled from the branch of the sacred sakaki tree beside the mirror that drew Amaterasu from her cave. Counted among the Three Sacred Treasures of Japan, it symbolizes benevolent fortune and the sovereign's mandate, and its comma shape recurs in tomb jewelry from the Kofun period.

name: Shichishito
powers: None (honorific and ritual sword)
description: An iron sword with seven branch-like projections along the blade, dedicated to the Isonokami Shrine and recorded in the Nihon Shoki as a gift from the kingdom of Baekje. Its long inlaid inscription describing offerings to the sun deity makes it a rare physical relic of early Korean-Japanese exchange and a treasure of Japanese shrine keeping.
